title: Cancellation with AbortController and AbortSignal.timeout; async iterators; debounce
summary: A Promise can't be cancelled, so the platform passes an AbortSignal into the work instead, much like Go's context. Pull-based async iterators and debouncing stop or skip work at the source.

annotations.note: What fetch does with a signal: on abort, stop the work and reject with signal.reason. Cancellation is cooperative, as with ctx.Done() in Go: a function that ignores its signal can't be cancelled.
throwIfAborted() throws the reason if the signal has already fired. Check before starting expensive work, as Go code checks ctx.Err().
Remove the listener when the work completes. A long-lived signal, one per page for example, would otherwise collect a listener per request.
e is unknown. The abort reasons the platform creates are DOMExceptions, and their name says why; a reason you pass yourself arrives as is.
The controller cancels and the signal observes, the same split as Go's context.WithCancel returning ctx and cancel. abort() without an argument makes the reason a DOMException named AbortError.
AbortSignal.timeout(ms) is context.WithTimeout. Its reason is a TimeoutError, so callers can tell "too slow" from "cancelled".
any() aborts when the first of its signals does, with that signal's reason. An aborted signal stays aborted: later calls fail at once, so new work needs a new controller.

examples.title: Async generators: break stops the producer, a signal stops it from outside

annotations.note: An async generator is pull-based: the next page is fetched only when the consumer asks for more items. Work nobody asks for never starts.
The cancellation check sits between pages, so cancellation takes effect at the next check: C was already fetched and still arrives after the abort at B.
finally runs however the loop ends: completion, break or a thrown error. This is where a real generator releases its reader, cursor or connection.
break makes for await call the generator's return(), which runs its finally: page 2 is never fetched. Go 1.23 iterators work the same way: yield returns false and the iterator must stop.
Cancellation from outside: the generator throws AbortError at its next check, runs finally, and the error surfaces at the for await loop.

examples.title: Search as you type: abort the previous request, debounce the input

annotations.note: Both sides are lowercased with the Turkish rules (İ to i, I to ı), so "izm" finds İzmir. Plain toLowerCase() turns İ into i plus a combining dot, and the prefix never matches.
Latest wins: each search aborts the one before. Without this, a slow answer for "a" could arrive after the answer for "ant" and overwrite the newer results.
Tell your own abort from a real failure by asking the signal, not by parsing the error. Real failures still propagate.
Debounce: each call clears the pending timer, so only a call followed by ms of quiet runs. There is no built-in; this is the whole thing.
Without debounce, three keystrokes start three requests and two are aborted. With it, the same three keystrokes start one.

use_cases: Leaving a page or closing a dialog: abort its requests so late responses don't update UI that is gone
Search as you type: debounce the input and abort the previous request
A deadline on any async call with AbortSignal.timeout, merged with a user's cancel through AbortSignal.any
Paginated APIs and streams consumed with for await and stopped early with break
Removing many event listeners at once: addEventListener(type, fn, { signal })
strengths: One standard cancellation token for fetch, event listeners, streams and your own functions, as context.Context is in Go, instead of a cancel() method per library
The reason says why: AbortError for abort(), TimeoutError for AbortSignal.timeout(), or any value you pass to abort(reason)
Async generators stop when the consumer stops: break runs the producer's finally, so cleanup sits next to the code that acquired the resource
weaknesses: Cooperative only: there is no promise.cancel(), and code that ignores its signal keeps running
Nothing passes the signal for you: every function in the chain needs a signal parameter, the same discipline as ctx in Go
Debounce and throttle are not built in, and a hand-written debounce needs a cancel path for when the UI goes away
AbortSignal.any() is recent: available in all major browsers only since 2024

pitfalls.title: Reporting an abort as an error
pitfalls.detail: An aborted request is the expected outcome of cancelling. Check the signal before showing an error message.

pitfalls.title: Reusing an aborted controller
pitfalls.detail: A signal is one-shot: once aborted it stays aborted, and every API given it rejects at once. Create a new AbortController per operation.

pitfalls.title: Rejecting without stopping the work
pitfalls.detail: An abort handler that only rejects leaves the timer, stream or socket running. Stop the work itself (clearTimeout, reader.cancel(), close) and remove the listener when the work completes.

pitfalls.title: Debounced calls that outlive their component
pitfalls.detail: The pending timer fires after the user navigated away. Keep a way to clear it, and call it from the effect cleanup together with abort().

quiz.q: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) }) takes too long. What is err.name in the catch block?
quiz.why: AbortSignal.timeout aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException, and fetch rejects with the signal's reason.

quiz.q: A for await loop over an async generator executes break. What happens to the generator?
options: It keeps fetching in the background
Its return() is called: its finally block runs and it stops
quiz.why: Leaving a for await loop early calls the iterator's return(), which resumes the generator at a return and runs its finally.

quiz.q: The user types i, iz, izm within 50 ms, into a box debounced at 50 ms. How many searches start?
quiz.why: Each call restarts the timer; only the last call is followed by 50 ms of quiet.

quiz.q: Search input is debounced. Why abort the previous request as well?
options: Debounce already cancels requests in flight
A request already sent can answer after a newer one and overwrite fresher results
Browsers allow only one fetch at a time
quiz.why: Debounce only decides when to start. Once two requests overlap, only aborting the old one guarantees the newest result is the one shown.

body:
## Concept

A Promise has no `cancel()`. The platform solves cancellation with a separate pair of
objects: an `AbortController`, which you keep, and its `AbortSignal`, which you pass into
the work. `controller.abort(reason)` marks the signal aborted, fires its `abort` event, and
every API holding the signal stops and rejects with `signal.reason`: `fetch`, streams,
`addEventListener` (the listener is removed), and your own functions if they listen.

Two factories cover the common cases: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts itself with a
`TimeoutError`, and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` aborts when the first of its inputs does.

Stopping work also happens at the source. An async generator produces items only when
the consumer asks, so breaking out of `for await` stops it, and its `finally` cleans up.
Debouncing delays work until the input stops changing, and "latest wins" aborts the
previous request when a new one starts.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Go**: `AbortController` plus `AbortSignal` is `cancel` plus `ctx` from
  `context.WithCancel`; `signal.aborted` is `ctx.Err() != nil`; the `abort` event is
  `<-ctx.Done()`; `signal.reason` is `context.Cause`; `AbortSignal.timeout` is
  `context.WithTimeout`. Signals carry no values and form no tree on their own:
  `AbortSignal.any` is how you derive one from several.
- **Java**: `Future.cancel(true)` interrupts a thread. There is no thread to interrupt here,
  so cancellation is a flag plus an event that the work must observe, like a hand-rolled
  `volatile boolean cancelled`.
- **Python**: `Task.cancel()` raises `CancelledError` inside the task at its next `await`,
  with no cooperation needed. JavaScript can't inject an exception into a running async
  function; the function has to check its signal.
- **JS**: `async function*` with `for await...of` (ES2018) is the async twin of generators
  and `for...of`. Leaving the loop early calls the iterator's `return()`, the hook that
  lets a producer clean up.

## Design notes

Give every async function that does I/O an optional `signal` and pass it down, for example
`load(id: string, { signal }: { signal?: AbortSignal } = {})`. It is the same discipline as
`ctx context.Context` as the first parameter in Go: tedious, explicit, and the only way
cancellation reaches the bottom of the stack.

Decide in one place what an abort means. Usually it means "nobody wants this result
anymore", which is not an error: don't log it, don't show it, don't retry it. A timeout,
on the other hand, often is an error worth reporting, which is why the two reasons have
different names.

For UI input, combine the tools: debounce decides *when* to start, aborting the previous
request decides *which* answer may render, and the component's cleanup aborts whatever is
still running when it goes away. The React effects lesson builds on exactly this.
